item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication.
item.description:
eLife
The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: Bridging brain structure and function: Structural-functional brain network coupling and frontal midline theta connectivity in general intelligence
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC), as well as their alignment (SC-FC coupling), may underlie individual differences in general intelligence. We hypothesized that intelligence emerges from optimized SC-FC coupling and additional processes, namely the task-dependent rapid regulation of FC. To test this hypothesis, we examined MRI-derived SC-FC coupling and EEG-derived midfrontal theta FC dynamics as complementary predictors of intelligence within a latent variable framework. We used a sample of 215 healthy adults (113 females) aged 18–40 years who underwent extensive cognitive ability testing and completed a conceptually similar cued task-switching task during EEG and functional MRI acquisition. Although we found no evidence for a broad association between whole-brain SC-FC coupling and intelligence, an exploratory analysis contrasting functional contexts revealed one for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling computed from task-evoked FC. Specifically, higher coupling predicted higher general intelligence, β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]. Regarding midfrontal theta connectivity, we found no evidence for an association with intelligence at a preregistered electrode (Fz). However, an exploratory analysis of a broader electrode cluster revealed a temporally specific effect, β = 0.36, 95% CI [0.05, 0.67], suggesting that intelligence may rely on flexible modulation of FC across successive stages of information processing. In a combined model, the two connectivity-based predictors showed no substantial correlation with each other, r = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.25], but both remained significant predictors of intelligence, β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.45] for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling and β = 0.22, 95% CI [0.06, 0.39] for late midfrontal theta connectivity. Together, both predictors explained 12.7% of variance in intelligence differences. These findings highlight that the connectivity–intelligence association may be spatially and temporally specific, while emphasizing that intelligence relies on multiple connectivity mechanisms spanning the brain’s structure and function.

item.title: Wisdom, mythology, and the prefrontal cortex: a neurocognitive interpretation of Athena's birth.
item.description:
Postgraduate medical journal
BACKGROUND: The myth of Athena's birth from Zeus' forehead presents a symbolic narrative that resonates with modern neuroscientific perspectives. The prefrontal cortex, crucial for decision-making, foresight, and moral reasoning, aligns intriguingly with the ancient attribution of wisdom to the head. This study aims to explore the convergence of mythology, philosophy, visual art, and neuroscience in order to examine whether ancient cultural narratives implicitly localized wisdom in the brain. METHODS: A multidisciplinary approach was employed, drawing on classical texts, iconographic traditions, and contemporary neurobiological models of wisdom.Comparative analysis was used to identify symbolic parallels between mythological representations and neurocognitive functions. RESULTS: The cranial emergence of Athena can be interpreted as a cultural archetype that anticipates the modern understanding of higher-order cognition. Artistic depictions reinforce this correspondence by emphasizing the head as the seat of wisdom. Despite the risk of anachronism, the recurrence of this imagery across centuries suggests that myth may encode latent insights into brain function. CONCLUSIONS: The case of Athena's birth highlights how mythological narratives can serve as proto-scientific frameworks for understanding human cognition. Integrating insights from mythology and neuroscience may enrich both historical interpretation and contemporary discussions on the nature of wisdom.

item.title: Motor system inefficiency as an activity-dependent amplifier of fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Multiple sclerosis (MS) fatigue is clinically obvious but mechanistically elusive. It can dominate daily life despite modest disability, stable structural MRI findings, or preserved strength on examination. This Update reviews evidence that an important component of MS fatigue may arise from increased motor-control cost and incomplete recovery after activity. Voluntary muscle activation studies show that some people with MS have incomplete central access to available force, particularly after exertion. Functional imaging studies indicate that apparently preserved movement often depends on expanded recruitment of premotor, cerebellar, striatal, prefrontal, and cingulo-insular systems involved in motor compensation, effort allocation, and body-state monitoring. Metabolic and pathological studies further indicate energetic vulnerability in demyelinated and chronically injured networks, providing biological plausibility for impaired restoration after repeated signalling demands. These findings support a systems framework in which expanded motor-control recruitment may be compensatory when it preserves performance and remains flexible and recoverable, but may amplify MS fatigue when ordinary activity begins from incompletely restored physiological reserve. We outline testable predictions for identifying a motor-cost fatigue phenotype and for designing repeated-measures studies of activity-related fatigue in MS.

item.title: Chronic and subacute phenylalanine effects on brain metabolism in adults with phenylketonuria.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Phenylketonuria (PKU) leads to chronic cerebral exposure to elevated phenylalanine (Phe) despite lifelong dietary treatment, yet the neurometabolic consequences in adulthood remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent alterations in brain metabolism and whether these metabolites respond dynamically to subacute Phe fluctuations. Adults with early-treated PKU (n=30) and healthy controls (n=59) underwent proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), structural and functional brain MRI to evaluate white matter lesion load (T2-weighted images) and cerebral blood flow (arterial spin labeling), as well as cognitive assessments. Patients additionally participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover intervention with four weeks of oral Phe loading to evaluate subacute metabolic responsiveness. Absolute metabolite concentrations were quantified in predominantly white matter tissue, and associations between blood and brain Phe, white matter lesion load, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance were examined. At baseline, patients exhibited higher brain Phe and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels, alongside reduced myo-inositol, N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), and total creatine/phosphocreatine compared with controls. Patients with white matter lesions did not differ in blood and brain metabolites from those without. Four weeks of oral Phe loading increased brain Phe and produced a reversible decrease in myo-inositol, whereas NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds remained unchanged. Blood and brain Phe concentrations were strongly correlated (r=0.83, p<0.001), and their ratio was subject-dependent. No significant associations were observed between metabolite concentrations and regional cerebral blood flow or cognitive performance after correction for multiple comparisons. Adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent neurometabolic alterations involving neuronal-glial metabolism, energy buffering, and astrocytic osmolyte regulation. The findings support a trait-state framework, with stable alterations in NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds reflecting long-standing metabolic changes, superimposed on a dynamically Phe-sensitive astrocytic response indexed by myo-inositol. The absence of strong associations with cerebral perfusion or cognition suggests that these alterations represent upstream biological processes not captured by macroscopic imaging or behavioral measures.

item.title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

item.title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

item.title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection (β = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection (β = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE (β = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction (β = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

item.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in the Executive Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks. Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187). Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use. Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Thalamocortical Network Dynamics During Focal Seizures in Humans.
item.description:
Neurology
The thalamus is an emerging neuromodulation target in drug-resistant focal epilepsy because of its frequent ictal involvement. However, frequency-specific and directional thalamocortical dynamics remain poorly understood. We sought to characterize thalamocortical network dynamics across seizure evolution using stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). We retrospectively analyzed SEEG recordings from patients with pediatric-onset drug-resistant focal epilepsy with simultaneous cortical and thalamic sampling focusing on the anterior nucleus (AN) and centromedian nucleus (CM). We applied visual analysis with quantitative measures of spectral power, imaginary coherence, and spectral Granger causality across slow (1-12 Hz), β (13-30 Hz), and γ (30-70 Hz) bands to quantify thalamocortical and cortico-cortical interactions from seizure onset to termination. Random forest models were trained to classify seizure state using thalamic EEG features as an exploratory analysis. The final cohort comprised 19 patients (median age, 16.9 years; 31.6% female), with 66 focal seizures analyzed. Thalamic ictal activity was present at seizure onset in 81% of sampled thalamic contacts and became nearly universal by seizure termination. Both the thalamus and seizure onset zone showed increased spectral power during seizures, with prominent slow-band augmentation at seizure termination in the thalamus. Similarly, thalamocortical imaginary coherence increased during seizures, with the largest changes near seizure termination in the slow band (AN-SOZ: 11% [IQR, 2 to 20], rank-biserial correlations (rrb) = 0.84; CM-SOZ: 12% [IQR, 3 to 23], rrb = 0.84) and β band (AN-SOZ: 5% [IQR, 0 to 12], rrb = 0.74; CM-SOZ: 8% [IQR, 2 to 15], rrb = 0.86). Directed connectivity analyses demonstrated bidirectional thalamocortical interactions, with large slow-frequency thalamus-to-SOZ outflow near seizure termination from both AN and CM, exceeding propagation-zone-to-SOZ cortico-cortical flow (both p < 0.01). Seizure state was classified using thalamic EEG features, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.825 for AN and 0.839 for CM. Human focal seizures engage frequency-specific and bidirectional thalamocortical interactions that evolve from onset to termination. These findings support the thalamus as a source of clinically relevant seizure-state information and may inform thalamic biomarker development for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy.

item.title: Immature Valence Recognition of Emotional Speech in Cochlear Implant Users: Evidence From Event-Related Potentials and Neural Oscillations.
item.description:
Ear and hearing
Objectives Rapid emotional perception in speech is crucial to efficient social communication. Cochlear implant (CI) users, constrained by device limitations in transmitting spectro-temporal detail, rely more on semantic than prosodic cues for emotional processing of spoken language. This study investigated whether CI users can rapidly recognize emotional valence based on semantic cues before full semantic comprehension when prosodic information is minimized. Design Chinese monosyllables with negative or positive valence were presented with neutral prosody using an oddball paradigm. Event-related potentials and neural oscillations were recorded in CI users and normal-hearing (NH) listeners. Results Emotional syllables evoked an N400, indicative of semantic processing, in NH listeners. Crucially, NH listeners showed an earlier mismatch negativity (MMN) for negative syllable deviants, reflecting rapid categorical perception of emotional valence. However, the N400 for positive deviants and the MMN were absent in CI users. Furthermore, compared with NH listeners, CI users showed weaker theta-band and alpha-band event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs) and inter-trial coherences and a greater beta-band ERSP. A lower beta-band ERSP was correlated with greater N400 and late negative component in NH listeners. Personality scores for extraversion and agreeableness correlated with the amplitudes of the MMN and N400 components, respectively. Conclusions The findings portray the dynamics of emotional speech processing and demonstrate that rapid recognition of emotional valence expressed by lexical meaning occurs before complete semantic processing in the NH brain. Theta activity may be associated with early emotional valence recognition, and beta activity corresponds to higher-level semantic and emotional processing. However, these two processes are immature in CI users, as evidenced by absent event-related potentials and altered neural oscillations. Personality traits may modulate emotional sensitivity, further affecting the efficiency of emotional speech processing.

item.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

item.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1, a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

item.title: Transferring active inference to newly encountered prism-shifted environments.
item.description:
Communications biology
Rapid adaptability to sudden changes in environmental contingencies is a hallmark of biological intelligence. However, how animals flexibly adapt to novel environments remains largely unclear. To investigate the brain's generalizability, this work focuses on prism adaptation, a classical visuomotor phenomenon reflecting rapid recalibration of perception-action coupling. Modeling is conducted based on canonical neural networks that instantiate active inference at the circuit level. Namely, we develop canonical neural networks equipped with multiple policy matrices in parallel, enabling the reuse of previously acquired sensorimotor knowledge. We demonstrate that the proposed model recapitulates key features of prism adaptation in an arm-reaching task, including rapid error reduction and after-effects following prism removal. Networks employing policies pretrained for different target positions adapt substantially faster than naive networks that relearn policies from scratch. These results suggest a biologically plausible mechanism by which neural circuits flexibly reuse prior knowledge to support rapid adaptation.

item.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

item.title: Brain predictors of episodic memory change across race/ethnic groups: A machine learning investigation.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
It is known that brain measures predict cognitive trajectories and that these predictions are not uniform across ethnoracial groups. But it remains unclear whether group differences reflect differing brain-cognition associations or similar associations but different demographic and brain health distributions. We used eXtreme Gradient Boosting regression tree modeling to predict episodic memory (EM) trajectories from 64 brain measures, including regional gray matter thickness and white matter tract diffusion-tensor free water, with age, sex, education, and ethnoracial indicators in four well-established, ethnically and racially diverse U.S.-based cohorts. eXtreme Gradient Boosting combines many simple regression trees to model nonlinear relationships among predictors and outcome; predictor importance was ranked using SHapley Additive exPlanation values. In a sample of 1,463 participants (mean age, 77.0 ± 8.4 years; 503 African American, 168 Asian, 289 Hispanic, and 503 White), a computationally based gray matter signature and white matter tract hippocampal cingulum free-water brain measures ranked first and second in global importance to predict EM trajectory, followed by uncinate fasciculus free water. Generalized additive model analyses by ethnoracial group and age strata showed equivalent pairwise SHapley Additive exPlanation-brain dependency curves for the top two brain measures. Mean absolute deviations were less than 5% of between-participant standard deviation for EM slope, indicating that brain-outcome SHapley Additive exPlanation dependencies were similar across age and ethnoracial groups. EM trajectory prediction profiles reflect different sample compositions of brain health measures rather than different brain-EM associations. This suggests that observed variability in brain-EM predictors derives from group-specific distributions of demographic predictors and brain health. item.title: Inter-subject functional variability of gray and white matter during methadone maintenance treatment and its association with gene expression profiles.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Methadone maintenance treatment(MMT) for opioid use disorder(OUD) may cause changes in brain functional heterogeneity whose molecular mechanisms remain unknown. This study aims to investigate MMT-related gray/white matter inter-subject variability functional connectivity(GM/WM-IVFC) alterations and to associate them with clinical and transcriptomic characteristics. Between March 2017 and June 2026, a total of 244 participants were voluntarily enrolled from detoxification centers, drug rehabilitation clinics, and society in Hunan Province, China, including MMT group(N = 44), individuals with sustained heroin self-abstinence and no lifetime MMT(HSA, N = 42), short-term abstinent heroin users at baseline(OUD1, N = 62) and 10-month opioid-free follow-up(OUD2, N = 43), and two healthy control cohorts(HC1, N = 48; HC2, N = 48) respectively age/gender-matched with MMT/HSA groups and OUD1. OUD1/2 and HSA groups were used to exploratively investigate the influence of previous heroin use and non-MMT abstinence duration on IVFC. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) data were acquired and analyzed to extract GM/WM-IVFC metrics, which were compared ROI-wise between groups and correlated with neuropsychological scales. Transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas(AHBA) were integrated via partial least squares(PLS) regression and functional enrichment analyses to further identify gene expression profiles underlying IVFC alterations. After Bonferroni correction, compared to HC1, MMT group exhibited the most widespread IVFC increases, spanning 20 GM and 7 WM regions. HSA group shared some overlapping GM-IVFC elevations with MMT group in bilateral orbital parts of inferior frontal gyrus and thalamus, yet its overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions was lower than that of MMT group. Neither OUD1 nor OUD2 showed difference in overall mean IVFC of significant GM regions from HC2. Both OUD1/2 displayed elevated overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions relative to HC2. Then, the overall mean IVFC of significant GM/WM regions between MMT group and HC1 were positively correlated with impulsivity, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and daily methadone dose. PLS regression linked IVFC patterns to AHBA transcriptomic profiles in MMT group, with enriched pathways in neuroinflammation, synaptic function, glutamatergic signaling, and neuronal development. item.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.

item.title: Corticospinal tract remodeling after stroke: Experimental mechanisms and implications for functional recovery.
item.description:
Neurobiology of disease
Recovery of voluntary motor function after stroke is strongly constrained by the integrity of the corticospinal tract (CST), a principal descending pathway controlling skilled and fractionated movements. Although ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke frequently disrupts CST projections, surviving corticospinal neurons retain a significant capacity for structural and functional remodeling. Understanding how this residual capacity contributes to recovery is therefore central to neurorestorative research. This narrative review synthesizes experimental and clinical findings to define the structural, cellular, molecular, and activity-dependent mechanisms underlying CST remodeling after stroke. Clinical studies using diffusion tensor imaging and transcranial magnetic stimulation demonstrate that CST integrity is a major determinant of recovery potential, forming the basis of widely used prognostic models. Experimental work, particularly in rodent stroke models, indicates that post-stroke CST remodeling commonly involves short-range axonal sprouting of spared corticospinal neurons within spinal gray matter, rather than long-distance regeneration across damaged white matter pathways. These structural changes are regulated by a complex interplay of intrinsic neuronal growth programs, myelin-associated inhibitory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, glial responses, and activity-dependent circuit selection. Importantly, CST remodeling occurs within a broader network of cortical, brainstem, and spinal adaptations and may contribute to restitution, compensation, or both depending on lesion severity and residual structural capacity. We further examine emerging pharmacological, gene-based, cell-based, neuromodulatory, environmental, and rehabilitation strategies designed to enhance or guide CST plasticity. Finally, we discuss biological heterogeneity, spontaneous recovery, experimental model limitations, and the challenges of translating preclinical CST remodeling into clinically meaningful restoration of dexterous motor function. Together, these findings support a framework in which structural reserve, the post-injury biological environment, and patterned activity interact to determine the functional value of CST remodeling and inform biologically stratified therapeutic approaches.

item.title: Multidimensional psycholinguistic difficulty in Cantonese picture naming: Behavioral, neural, and effective connectivity evidence.
item.description:
Brain and language
Picture naming is a useful paradigm for studying spoken word production because it requires the transformation of visual object input into a lexical response through coordinated conceptual and lexical processes. This study examined whether inherent psycholinguistic difficulty in picture naming is multidimensional or unitary. Thirty-eight healthy native Cantonese speakers performed an overt object picture-naming task during fMRI. Four psycholinguistic variables were modeled: conceptual familiarity, average neighborhood distance (AND), naming disagreement, and lexical frequency. Mixed-effects models showed that higher conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency facilitated naming, whereas higher AND increased both errors and response times; naming disagreement increased errors but did not significantly affect response times. Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency on response times, indicating the facilitative effect of frequency was modulated by familiarity. For errors, significant interactions were found between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency, as well as between AND and lexical frequency, and between AND and naming disagreement, revealing complex joint influences on naming accuracy. Whole-brain analyses revealed dissociable neural effects across variables. Conjunction analysis showed that lower conceptual familiarity and higher AND converged in bilateral lateral occipital and ventral occipitotemporal regions, with extension into the left posterior temporal cortex, suggesting shared sensitivity to semantic-level difficulty. In contrast, naming disagreement and lexical frequency did not show significant lexical-level overlap. Effective connectivity analyses further identified a stable directed ROI architecture during naming. Together, the findings support a multidimensional account of picture-naming difficulty in which semantic- and lexical-related item properties impose partially distinct but interacting constraints on spoken word production.

item.title: A hierarchical study of depression and subcortical gray matter volume in adults with HIV.
item.description:
Journal of neurovirology
Depression is highly prevalent in people with HIV (PWH). However, brain imaging studies of depression in PWH have been rather limited. We used a hierarchical approach to systematically investigate the impact of depression on subcortical volume in adults with HIV, focusing on the medial temporal lobe (MTL), the basal ganglia (BG), and the diencephalon. 99 PWH were included in the analysis (41-70 years old, 65% Black/African American, 25% female). Depression status was determined via the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Gray matter volume (GMv) of MTL, BG, diencephalon, and their subfields were estimated using FreeSurfer (v8.0.0). Linear regressions were performed in a hierarchical fashion to examine the association between depression and GMv of subcortical regions and subregions. The impacts of clinical and demographic factors were also examined. Depression was associated with lower GMv in the MTL (p = 0.014), but not the BG (p = 0.179) or diencephalon (p = 0.264). For subfields, depression was strongly associated with lower GMv in the hippocampal formation and most of its subfields, as well as in the basolateral and cortical-like regions and subnuclei of the amygdala. None of the viral factors were associated with any significant changes in GMv, including detectable viral load, nadir CD4, current CD4 count, and disease duration. In PWH, depression was associated with lower subcortical GMv, especially within the hippocampal formation and the basolateral amygdala, largely in accordance with the general population. Future longitudinal studies are needed to answer whether these associations continue or even grow throughout aging, and whether clinical factors play a role.

item.title: Spatial and functional organization of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) during cue and execution of motor tasks.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The primary motor cortex has traditionally been conceptualized as a somatotopically organized structure, with discrete cortical regions corresponding to specific body parts. However, accumulating evidence suggests that motor cortex organization extends beyond simple effector-based representations to include higher-order functional systems supporting goal-directed behavior. Here, we examine the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN), a set of inter-effector cortical regions located between the classical hand, foot, and face representations of primary motor cortex that has been proposed to integrate cognitive control processes with motor function. Using task-based functional MRI during a motor paradigm that dissociates cue-related and execution-related processes, we investigated the functional role and spatial organization of SCAN in healthy adults. SCAN exhibited preferential activation during the cue phase, greater than during movement execution, indicating a prominent role in action preparation rather than motor output. In contrast, classical effector-specific motor representations corresponding to individual body parts (hand, foot, and face) showed greater engagement during execution, consistent with their role in movement generation. Across these SCAN regions, activation increased systematically from dorsomedial regions (adjacent to leg representations) to ventrolateral regions (adjacent to face representations). This spatial gradient was accompanied by progressively greater dominance of preparatory SCAN activity relative to movement-related activity in the adjacent effector regions. Together, these findings demonstrate that motor cortex organization includes a distinct integrative system that is temporally and spatially dissociable from effector-specific representations. These results support an integrate-isolate framework in which cognitive and motor processes are differentially expressed across the cortical landscape, providing new insight into the functional architecture of human motor control.

item.title: Speech and Language Abnormalities in Putative Brain-First Versus Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
The α-synuclein origin model proposes brain-first and body-first Parkinson's disease (PD) subtypes, with speech potentially revealing their distinct neurodegenerative patterns. We aimed to analyze the possible speech and language differences between untreated PD patients with premotor (putative body-first) and without (putative brain-first) rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Speech samples of reading passages and monologues were automatically analyzed using acoustic and linguistic features. We enrolled 23 body-first and 35 brain-first de novo PD patients compared with 35 healthy controls. Brain-first patients showed greater speech impairment severity compared with body-first patients (P = 0.002) and controls (P < 0.001), whereas body-first patients showed greater language impairment severity compared with brain-first patients (P < 0.001) and controls (P < 0.001). Putative brain-first subtype had more motor speech abnormalities whereas body-first subtype manifested greater language impairment. Thes finding is consistent with motor-dominant nigrostriatal involvement in brain-first and broader non-motor/cognitive involvement in body-first PD. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: EPHB2 promotes long-range axon extension and its variants cause callosal dysgenesis
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest fibre tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres, essential for integrating neural activity across large-scale brain networks. Accordingly, abnormal CC development is associated with diverse neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) of the cortex form the CC by extending long-range axons to the contralateral hemisphere; however, the mechanisms that sustain axon elongation over such remarkable distances remain poorly understood. Here we show that variants in the human gene EPHB2, which encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor regulating nervous system development and implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, cause CC dysgenesis. We characterise variant- specific effects on EPHB2 signalling and demonstrate that variants identified in individuals with distinct CC morphologies differentially alter CPN axon outgrowth and integration in vivo. We further show that EphB2 has a cell-autonomous, ligand-independent function in promoting CPN axon outgrowth by spatially organising actomyosin at axonal growth cones. These findings reveal a previously unrecognised role for EphB2 in promoting long-range axon extension and provide the first evidence that EPHB2 variants cause CC dysgenesis in humans. More broadly, our study links molecular variation in EPHB2 to individualised abnormalities in brain connectivity and provides a framework for understanding how heterogeneous circuit-level phenotypes arise in neurodevelopmental disorders.

item.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

item.title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

item.title: Oligodendroglial Dysfunction in Cognitive Aging: Myelin-Axon Integrity and Functional Repair.
item.description:
Aging and disease
Oligodendrocytes sustain brain function by maintaining myelin and providing metabolic support to axons. Aging can compromise both functions, yet changes in myelin abundance do not necessarily reflect the extent of axonal dysfunction or cognitive decline. Here, we compare human and experimental evidence for structural, metabolic, electrophysiological, and functional differences between myelin preservation and axonal performance, and relate these findings to cognitive aging. We discuss approaches to restore oligodendrocyte renewal and preserve mature-cell function, together with the barriers imposed by the aging tissue environment. The goal of repair should extend beyond increasing myelin to restoring axonal function and achieving sustained cognitive benefit.

item.title: Association of scan time with resting-state functional connectivity discriminability: effects of temporal alignment.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is increasingly used to probe individual differences in brain organization, but individual-level FC discriminability may vary across repeated acquisitions related to arousal, physiology, and endogenous brain state. Acquisition-time variation may be a systematic contributor to this variability, yet its impact on FC discriminability has not been well characterized. Multi-session resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project were analyzed using minimally preprocessed and ICA-FIX-denoised BOLD time series. Whole-brain and network-level FC matrices were constructed after atlas-based parcellation, and sessions were grouped into one-hour daytime bins. Discriminability was computed to quantify how well repeated FC profiles from the same individual could be distinguished from those of other individuals, and grouped versus ungrouped estimates were compared. Temporal alignment of scans according to acquisition time substantially improved FC discriminability across both test-retest configurations. Whole-brain discriminability increased from 0.29 to 0.61 in one configuration and from 0.31 to 0.60 in the other. Similar gains were observed across canonical networks, with robust improvements in the default mode, dorsal attention, frontoparietal, and visual networks. These findings show that acquisition-time grouping was associated with higher FC discriminability in this HCP sample. Incorporating acquisition-time structure into rs-fMRI acquisition and analysis may enhance connectome fingerprinting and improve FC discriminability.

item.title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. Methods High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. Results Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Conclusion Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

item.title: The disrupted navigational compass: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical interventions for spatial navigation deficits.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Spatial navigation is a higher-order integrative cognitive ability that supports environmental orientation, goal-directed route selection, and adaptive locomotion by integrating spatial memory, multisensory cues, attention, and executive control. Neural systems supporting navigation are also vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease, making navigation a useful domain for linking basic mechanisms with clinically measurable functional impairment. This review summarizes spatial-navigation mechanisms across multiple levels. At the cognitive level, navigation depends on interacting processes including spatial representation, path integration, reference-frame transformation, landmark use, and route planning. At the network level, hippocampal-entorhinal, retrosplenial-parietal, scene-selective, and prefrontal systems contribute complementary functions. At the cellular level, place-, grid-, head-direction-, speed-, and boundary-related representations encode position, heading, self-motion, environmental geometry, and prospective behavior. Clinical and neuroimaging studies indicate that navigation impairment is associated with structural and functional abnormalities, with the strongest diagnostic evidence currently arising from Alzheimer's disease and its prodromal stages. VR-based behavioral assessment and electrophysiological approaches provide complementary means of characterizing navigation phenotypes: VR enables controlled, repeatable, process-sensitive tasks, whereas intracranial and scalp recordings provide neural information at different spatial and physiological scales. No pharmacological agent has been developed or licensed specifically for navigation impairment; current navigation-focused interventions therefore rely mainly on behavioral and VR-based rehabilitation, compensatory strategies, and emerging neuromodulation approaches. Future studies should integrate process-specific behavioral and physiological markers with biomarker-defined clinical cohorts, and use large, randomized, longitudinal studies to establish diagnostic validity, real-world transfer, and mechanism-informed intervention effects.

item.title: Cortical Macro- and Microstructural Alterations in Multiple System Atrophy and Their Clinical Correlates.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Background Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is primarily characterized by subcortical neurodegeneration. However, neuropathological evidence indicates that cortical neurodegeneration is also part of the disease. Conventional neuroimaging measures, such as cortical thickness (CTh), have been used to assess cortical macrostructural alterations, but findings remain limited and inconclusive. In this context, cortical mean diffusivity (cMD) has emerged as a promising marker of microstructural integrity, capturing alterations beyond macrostructural changes in other neurodegenerative disorders. However, its role in MSA remains largely unexplored. Objectives The objective of the study was to characterize cortical macro- and microstructural alterations in MSA and assess associations with clinical severity and cognitive performance. Methods T1-weighted and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), clinical, and neuropsychological assessments were obtained in 29 patients with MSA and 35 age- and sex-matched controls (HCs). Cortical macro- and microstructural alterations were evaluated using CTh and cMD, respectively. Group comparisons and correlations between MRI-derived cortical measures and clinical, cognitive, and neurodegeneration biomarkers were conducted (P < 0.05, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected). Results Patients with MSA exhibited widespread increases in cMD, predominantly affecting the frontal and temporal cortices. This pattern partially overlapped with cortical thinning, although cMD alterations extended to rostral-lateral, rostral-medial, and inferior-medial regions. In MSA, increased cMD was associated with global cognitive impairment, whereas cortical thinning correlated with disease severity. Conclusions MSA involves concurrent macro- and microstructural cortical alterations, with microstructural changes potentially preceding overt atrophy and indicating early pathology. Distinct cMD and CTh patterns suggest partially independent processes, whereas differential clinical associations highlight their complementarity. Together, these markers improve the characterization of cortical degeneration and disease heterogeneity. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Heterogeneous Negative Gray Matter Volume Deviations Converge on a Shared Depression Circuit Associated With Symptoms and rTMS Response.
item.description:
Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by marked heterogeneity in regional negative gray matter volume (GMV) deviations, obscuring the network basis of the disorder. Here, subject-specific normative GMV deviation maps are integrated with the human connectome using atrophy network mapping. Extreme negative GMV deviations in a medication-naive, first-episode MDD discovery cohort (n = 105) and an independent multisite validation cohort (n = 1265) converge on a reproducible depression circuit characterized by positive connectivity with subcortical-limbic regions and negative connectivity with frontoparietal and default mode network hubs. Circuit coupling tracks depressive symptom severity, follows gradients of depression-risk gene expression, and shows preliminary translational relevance: stronger negative connectivity at individualized rTMS targets is associated with greater clinical improvement. These findings reconcile heterogeneous structural deviations with the shared MDD phenotype and may inform future circuit-based neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Complex Spatial and Temporal Organization of Functional Brain Networks
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent research exploring brain-behavior associations has relied on the language of complex systems to understand how stable behavioral individual differences emerge from brain function. At the same time, advances in neuroimaging have provided greater insight into both the topological and temporal properties of macroscale cortical networks. These new approaches offer a potential avenue for understanding how functional activity in the brain might behave in a manner that aligns with complex-systems interpretations of psychological traits. The present study used resting-state data from the Human Connectome project (N = 994) to explore associations between the spatial and temporal features of functional brain networks. Using an adaptive frequency approach to explore brain function at different timescales together with a family of methods from complex systems theory, we identified patterns of brain state organization reflecting a state-trait continuum, with more stable trait-like dynamics and greater functional coupling between networks in lower frequency oscillations. Additionally, we found evidence of greater coupling across timescales in brain networks associated with higher-order cognition. This research supports interpretations of brain organization as a spatiotemporal hierarchy and provides future avenues for exploring brain-behavior associations from a complex system perspective.

item.title: Neurophysiological evidence for rapid semantic integration via fast mapping.
item.description:
Cognitive, affective & behavioral neuroscience
Theories of declarative memory consolidation hold that novel associative information is integrated into cortical semantic networks slowly and with hippocampal support. However, an encoding paradigm called fast mapping (FM) has been proposed to permit rapid cortical integration of novel item-label associations, particularly when the novel item shares substantial visual-semantic features with a simultaneously presented known concept. We tested whether associations encoded through FM immediately engage semantic memory networks, indexed by the N400 event-related potential. In contrast to behavioral semantic priming tasks, in which semantic relatedness and response congruency may be confounded, the present EEG study provides a more process-specific test of rapid semantic integration. Sixty participants encoded pairs of a novel item and an unfamiliar label under two conditions, differing with respect to the visual-semantic overlap between the novel item and a simultaneously presented known item. In a subsequent semantic priming task, the novel labels served as primes for semantically related versus unrelated targets. While behavioral results did not reveal a significant priming effect, EEG data indicated an N400 priming effect in the high-overlap FM condition, characterized by reduced N400 amplitudes for related compared with unrelated targets over a parietal electrode cluster. Crucially, the N400 effect was significantly larger after high-overlap FM than after low-overlap FM encoding, indicating that high feature overlap enhances rapid semantic integration already minutes after learning. These findings provide the first neurophysiological evidence that high-overlap FM enables rapid semantic integration.

item.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.
